title: 1dfuonm
The Disagreement over Mut'a Marriage (Temporary Marriage)
hook: How did a word of a verse and a practice in the Prophet's time open into two readings of jurisprudence?
scenes.0.text: Nisâ 4:24, speaking of the women whom it is lawful to marry, says that the women benefited from must be given their dowries as an obligation. The verse's word "istemte'tum" describes, in the Ja'fari reading, a marriage of fixed duration, mut'a. The same word has also been read as ordinary marriage and dowry.
scenes.1.text: In al-Tabari's commentary, a reading is reported from some Companions such as Ibn Abbas, Ubayy b. Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud in which the phrase "for a specified term" is added to the verse. This addition is not counted as Qur'anic text. The Ja'fari school continues to read Nisâ 24 as a marriage of fixed duration.
scenes.2.text: Mut'a was practiced in the Prophet's time, especially on expeditions. According to what is transmitted from Jabir b. Abdillah, the Prophet's herald came and announced permission to benefit. Jabir relates that the practice continued in the time of Caliph Abu Bakr and in the early period of Caliph Umar. The Ja'fari school continues this early practice as a marriage of fixed duration.
scenes.3.text: A narration about the day of Khaybar says that the Prophet forbade mut'a and the meat of domestic donkeys. This is a report from Imam Ali to Ibn Abbas. Muslim 1406 relates that permission was given in the year of the conquest of Mecca, and then it was said, "God has made this forbidden until the Day of Resurrection." Some narrations place the prohibition at Awtas or the Farewell Pilgrimage; the narrations do not agree with one another on the date. The Ja'fari school continues the permitted practice of the Prophet's time as a marriage of fixed duration.
scenes.3.art.actors.0.label: 19izoul
The Prophet
scenes.4.text: It is reported that in a speech of Caliph Umar he said he was forbidding two mut'as, the hajj tamattu' and mut'a with women, and that he would punish whoever did them. The sentence "Both existed in the Prophet's time" appears in the parallels of the narration; the exact wording must be checked separately. The Ja'fari school continues mut'a with women according to the Prophet's practice prior to this statement.
scenes.4.art.actors.0.label: 1nai5fq
Caliph Umar
scenes.5.text: The saying "Had Caliph Umar not forbidden it, only a wretched person would resort to fornication" is attributed to Imam Ali. A similar expression is also mentioned through Ibn Abbas and Ata in Abd al-Razzaq's Musannaf and in al-Tabari's commentary. Whether the saying belongs to Imam Ali or to Ibn Abbas, and its chain and authenticity, are disputed. Since the primary text has not been seen, no definitive ruling of authenticity has been given. The Ja'fari school continues mut'a according to the permission in the Prophet's time.
scenes.5.art.actors.0.label: lhg99z
Imam Ali
scenes.6.text: It is reported that Ibn Abbas permitted mut'a. This fatwa is tied to conditions such as necessity and a scarcity of women. The report that Ibn Abbas later abandoned it entirely comes through weak chains (Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari). Mut'a is a temporary marriage made between two adults with a fixed term and dowry. There is no divorce. When the term ends, the woman observes an iddah. It is not described as a secret deception. The Ja'fari reading reads Nisâ 24 as a marriage of fixed duration. The Sunni reading reads the same word as ordinary marriage and dowry. In Muslim 1405d, Jabir says the practice continued in the time of the Prophet and Abu Bakr and that Umar forbade it. In Muslim 1406a, Sabra relates that it was said they were permitted and then told to leave it. In Bukhari 4216, Imam Ali reports the prohibition on the day of Khaybar to Ibn Abbas. From whom the prohibition came and on which day varies according to the narrations. Al-Nawawi says there is consensus. The Ja'fari school does not accept this. It cannot be said that all schools today regard it as lawful.
sunni.0.says: At the battle of Khaybar the Prophet forbade mut'a and the meat of domestic donkeys; Imam Ali reports this to Ibn Abbas.
sunni.1.says: Ibn Abbas permits mut'a; his student says this was tied to difficult conditions such as a scarcity of women. Secondary report; the primary text was not read in this study.
sunni.2.says: Permission is given in the year of the conquest; then it is said, "God has made this forbidden until the Day of Resurrection." Narration of Sabra b. Ma'bad. 1406a: in the permitted mut'a, the Prophet saying, "Whoever has such a woman in hand, let him leave her."
sunni.3.says: The Prophet's herald comes and announces that permission to benefit has been given.
sunni.4.says: The hajj mut'a and the women's mut'a; Caliph Umar says he forbids both and will punish. The text was read on hadithunlocked; the sentence "the two mut'as existed in the Prophet's time" appears in the parallels of this narration, and the exact wording should be checked separately.
sunni.5.says: The narration saying "Mut'a was at the beginning of Islam"; it is said to have become forbidden by verse 23:6.
sunni.5.grade: Ali al-Za'i: weak; Ibn Hajar: weak and shadh, the chain is broken
sunni.6.says: An evaluation of the mut'a narrations and of the narrations of Ibn Abbas's retraction.
sunni.7.says: Al-Nawawi states that mut'a was forbidden after being permitted and is forbidden by consensus; al-Tabari comments on the verse. Page/number to be checked.
shia.0.says: The conditions of mut'a: a fixed term, a fixed dowry; the woman's iddah.
shia.0.grade: UNVERIFIED (secondary attribution from al-islam.org: vol. 5, p. 453)
shia.1.says: The rulings and narrations on mut'a.
shia.2.says: A compilation gathering Shia narrations, in all of whose chapter titles the term "mut'a" appears.
shia.3.says: The Imamiyya claim of consensus on the permissibility of mut'a, and its evidence.
shia.4.says: The narration of the reading "ila ajalin musamma" in 4:24 from Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and others.
shia.4.grade: SECONDARY: from a partisan article; primary text not seen
disputes.0.title: ro6d2
What does "istemte'tum" and Nisâ 4:24 mean?
disputes.0.shia: The word "istemte'tum" in Nisâ 4:24 is read together with the dowry in both traditions. The Ja'fari reading takes it as a marriage of fixed duration; the "specified term" reading is also used as support for this meaning.
disputes.0.sunni: The word "istemte'tum" in Nisâ 4:24 is read together with the dowry in both traditions. In the Sunni reading, the word is benefiting from ordinary marriage; additional readings are not counted as Qur'anic text, and the limit in 23:6 is also mentioned as marriage and concubinage.
disputes.1.title: 7zv7ci
Was the permission lifted?
disputes.1.shia: That permission for mut'a was given in the Prophet's time is mentioned in both sources. The Ja'fari school ties the prohibition to Caliph Umar's statement and does not accept that the verse and the Prophet's permission were lifted by it.
disputes.1.sunni: That permission for mut'a was given in the Prophet's time is mentioned in both sources. In the Sunni account, the permission is regarded as abrogated by the narrations of Khaybar, the Conquest, Awtas and the Farewell Pilgrimage (Bukhari 5115, Muslim 1406); there is a difference in the date, and in the end the ruling of prohibition is adopted.
disputes.2.title: g0tmev
To whom is Caliph Umar's prohibition attributed?
disputes.2.shia: Caliph Umar's speech forbidding the two mut'as also appears in Muslim. The Ja'fari reading ties the prohibition to his own statement and takes the permission of the Prophet's time as the basis.
disputes.2.sunni: Caliph Umar's speech forbidding the two mut'as also appears in Muslim. In the Sunni account, he reminded people of the prohibition the Prophet had set and enforced it; in some narrations, the knowledge of the prohibition reached him later.
questions.0: Muslim 1217 relates that Caliph Umar forbade the two mut'as. The sentence "It existed in the Prophet's time" appears in the parallels of the narration. How does this account make you think about the period to which the prohibition is tied?
questions.1: The date of the prohibition is told differently as Khaybar, the Conquest, Awtas and the Farewell Pilgrimage. What does this difference in date make you attend to when reading abrogation narrations?
questions.2: Jabir relates that the practice continued into the time of Caliph Abu Bakr and the early period of Caliph Umar (Muslim 1405). How does such a long continuation of the early practice shape how one reads the history of jurisprudence?
questions.3: The narration that ties Ibn Abbas's fatwa to hardship and the narration that says he retracted stand side by side. How does one look at the chains to understand the final form of a Companion's fatwa?
questions.4: The source and chain of the saying "Had Caliph Umar not forbidden it" are disputed. What weight does a saying whose chain is not clear carry on the subject of mut'a?
summary: Mut'a, as a marriage practiced in the Prophet's time, is also mentioned in Sunni books. Ja'fari jurisprudence continues it with the conditions of a fixed term, dowry and iddah. In the Sunni schools, it is regarded as forbidden by the later narrations of prohibition.
key: Mut'a: it existed in the Prophet's time
notes.0: Mut'a is a marriage for a term and is associated with Nisâ 4:24.
notes.1: That it was practiced on expeditions in the Prophet's time appears in the sources of both schools.
notes.2: In Sunni sources it is reported that it was later forbidden (dates such as Khaybar and the conquest of Mecca).
notes.3: Caliph Umar's speech of prohibition appears in Muslim 1217.
notes.4: In Ja'fari jurisprudence it continues with conditions. It is regarded as forbidden in the four Sunni schools; what is common is that it was practiced in the Prophet's time.
